question: If $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta$ are zeroes of the polynomial equation $x^{4}-3 x^{2}+6 x-12=0$ then the value of $\frac{\alpha+\beta+\gamma}{\delta^{2}}+\frac{\alpha+\delta+\gamma}{\beta^{2}}$ $+\frac{\alpha+\beta+\delta}{\gamma^{2}}$ $+\frac{\delta+\beta+\gamma}{\alpha^{2}}=$

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Given equation $x^{4}-3x^{2}+6x-12=0$ ...(i) On comparing with $ax^{4}+bx^{3}+cx^{2}+dx+e=0$ $a=1,\ b=0,\ c=-3,\ d=6,\ e=-12$ Since $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$ are the zeroes of the polynomial equation, $\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta=\frac{-b}{a}=0$ $\Rightarrow \alpha+\beta+\gamma=-\delta,\ \alpha+\delta+\gamma=-\beta$ and $\alpha+\beta+\delta=-\gamma,\ \delta+\beta+\gamma=-\alpha$ Also, $\sum\alpha\beta\gamma=\frac{-d}{a}=-6$ and $\alpha\beta\gamma\delta=\frac{e}{a}=-12$ Now consider, $\frac{\alpha+\beta+\gamma}{\delta^{2}}+\frac{\alpha+\delta+\gamma}{\beta^{2}}+\frac{\alpha+\beta+\delta}{\gamma^{2}}+\frac{\delta+\beta+\gamma}{\alpha^{2}}$ $=\frac{-\delta}{\delta^{2}}+\frac{-\beta}{\beta^{2}}+\frac{-\gamma}{\gamma^{2}}+\frac{-\alpha}{\alpha^{2}}$ $=-\frac{1}{\delta}-\frac{1}{\beta}-\frac{1}{\gamma}-\frac{1}{\alpha}$ $=-\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}+\frac{1}{\beta}+\frac{1}{\gamma}+\frac{1}{\delta}\right)$ $=-\left(\frac{\alpha\beta\gamma+\alpha\gamma\delta+\alpha\beta\delta+\beta\gamma\delta}{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}\right)$ $=-\left(\frac{\sum\alpha\beta\gamma}{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}\right)$ $=-\left(\frac{-6}{-12}\right)$ $=-\frac{1}{2}$ Hence the value of the given expression is $-\frac{1}{2}$ , which corresponds to option (1). © examsnet.com

question: A cylinder of mass $12\;\mathrm{kg}$ is sliding on plane with an initial velocity $20\;\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ . If the coefficient of friction between the surface and the cylinder is $0.5$ , before stopping. the cylinder describes a distance of ______

solution: Solution: Given that, mass of cylinder, $m = 12\;\mathrm{kg}$ Initial velocity, $u = 20\;\mathrm{m/s}$ Coefficient of friction, $\mu = 0.5$ We know that, the retardation produced by friction $a = -\mu g$ $= -0.5 \times 10$ $= -5\;\mathrm{m/s}^2$ [using, $g = 10\;\mathrm{m/s}^2$ ] Let $S$ be the distance travelled by cylinder to stop. question: A body of mass $M$ is dropped from a height $h$ on a sand floor. If the body penetrates $x \text{ cm}$ into the sand, the average resistance offered by the sand to the body is ______

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Given, mass of body $=M$ Height above the sand floor $=h$ Distance penetrated into sand $=x$ Let $v$ be the velocity with which body strikes the surface. Then, by equation of motion, we get $v^{2}=u^{2}+2 g h \Rightarrow v^{2}=2 g h$ ...(i) $[\because$ Initial velocity at highest point, $u=0]$ With this velocity $v$ , when body passes through the sand floor it comes to rest after travelling a distance $x$ . Let $F$ be the resisting force acting on body. Then, net downward force will be $F_{\text{net}}=Mg-F$ By work-energy theorem, work done by all forces is equal to change in $\text{KE}$ , which gives $W = \Delta K$ $F_{\text{net}} \times x = K_f - K_i$ $(Mg-F) x = 0 - \frac{1}{2} M v^{2}$ $[\because \text{ Final KE, } K_f = 0]$ $(Mg-F) x = -\frac{1}{2} M v^{2}$ ...(ii) Substituting the value from Eq. (i) in Eq. (ii), we get $\Rightarrow Mg x - F x = -\frac{1}{2} M (2 g h)$ $\Rightarrow Mg x - F x = -Mg h$ $\Rightarrow F x = Mg x + Mg h$ $\Rightarrow F = Mg \left( \frac{x+h}{x} \right)$ © examsnet.com

question: A disc of mass $4\text{ kg}$ and radius $0.4\text{ m}$ is rotating with angular velocity $30\text{ rads}^{-1}$ . When two point-masses, each $0.25\text{ kg}$ , are attached on the periphery of the disc, at diametrically opposite points, its angular velocity becomes _______

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Given, mass of disc, $M=4\text{ kg}$ Radius of disc, $R=0.4\text{ m}$ Initial angular velocity of disc, $\omega_{1}=30\text{ rad s}^{-1}$ Mass of point-masses, $m=0.25\text{ kg}$ Now, moment of inertia of disc, $I_{3}=\frac{1}{2}MR^{2}$ Moment of inertia of disc and two point mass system, $I_{2}=\frac{1}{2}MR^{2}+2mR^{2}$ Let $\omega_{2}$ be the final angular velocity. According to conservation of angular momentum, $I_{1}\omega_{1}=I_{2}\omega_{2}\Rightarrow\omega_{2}=\frac{I_{1}\omega_{1}}{I_{2}}$ Substituting the values, we get $\omega_{2}=\frac{\frac{1}{2}MR^{2}(30)}{\frac{1}{2}MR^{2}+2mR^{2}}$ $=\frac{\frac{1}{2}\times4\times(0.4)^{2}\times30}{\frac{1}{2}\times4\times(0.4)^{2}+2\times0.25\times(0.4)^{2}}$ $\omega_{2}=24\text{ rad/s}$ Hence, the final angular velocity of system is $24\text{ rad/s}$ . © examsnet.com

question: If rotational inertia parameter of a body rolling down a rough inclined plane (of inclination $\theta$ and height $h$ ) without slipping is given by $\beta = \frac{I_{CM}}{MR^{2}}$ , then time taken by the body to reach the bottom of the inclined plane is given by ______

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Given, mass of body $=M$ Radius $=R$ Angle of inclination $=\theta$ Height of inclined surface $=h$ Also, $\beta = \frac{I_{CM}}{MR^{2}}$ Using, the acceleration produced in body rolling down the inclined plane $a = \frac{g \sin\theta}{1+\frac{I_{CM}}{MR^{2}}} = \frac{g \sin\theta}{1+\beta}$ By using equation of motion, $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ where $u = 0$ (initial velocity) $t =$ time taken to reach at bottom. $s = 0 + \frac{1}{2} \frac{g \sin\theta}{(1+\beta)} t^{2}$ $\Rightarrow t^{2} = \frac{2 s (1+\beta)}{g \sin\theta}$ But, from the diagram, $\frac{h}{s} = \sin\theta$ $\Rightarrow s = \frac{h}{\sin\theta}$ Substituting the value of $s$ , we get $t = \sqrt{\frac{2 h (1+\beta)}{g \sin^{2}\theta}}$ $= \frac{1}{\sin\theta} \sqrt{\frac{2 h (1+\beta)}{g}}$ © examsnet.com

question: A bob of a pendulum of length $0.5\ \mathrm{m}$ has a speed of $6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at its lowest point. Find the speed of the bob when the string of the pendulum makes $60^{\circ}$ with the vertical. (take $g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ )

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Given, length of pendulum, $l=0.5\ \mathrm{m}$ Speed at lowest point, $v_{1}=6\ \mathrm{m/s}$ Angle made by string with vertical, $\theta=60^{\circ}$ In $\Delta OBC,\ \frac{OC}{OB}=\cos\theta=\cos 60^{\circ}$ $\frac{l-h}{l}=\cos 60^{\circ}$ $\Rightarrow h =l(1-\cos 60^{\circ})$ $\Rightarrow h =0.5\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\right)=0.25\ \mathrm{m}$ Using law of conservation of mechanical energy, we get $K_{i}+U_{i}=K_{f}+U_{f}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} m v_{1}^{2}+0=\frac{1}{2} m v_{2}^{2}+m g h$ [Taking initial potential energy at ground is equal to zero.] $\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} m v_{2}^{2} =\frac{1}{2} m v_{1}^{2}-m g h$ $\Rightarrow v_{2}^{2} =v_{1}^{2}-2 g h$ Substituting the values, we get $v_{2} =\sqrt{(6)^{2}-2\times10\times0.25}$ $=\sqrt{31}\ \mathrm{m/s}$ Hence, the final velocity at an angle $60^{\circ}$ is $\sqrt{31}\ \mathrm{m/s}$ . © examsnet.com

question: The radius of earth is about $6400 \text{km}$ and that of mars is $3200 \text{km}$ . And mass of the earth is about 10 times mass of mars. An object weighs $200 \text{N}$ on the surface of earth. Then its weight on the surface of mars will be ______

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Given, radius of Earth and Mars are $6400 \text{km}$ and $3200 \text{km}$ , respectively. Mass of Earth $=10$ (Mass of Mars) $M_e = 10 M_m$ We know that, acceleration due to gravity at surface of a planet is $g = \frac{GM}{R^2},$ where, $M =$ mass of planet and $R =$ radius of planet. Taking the ratio of acceleration due to gravity of Mars to Earth, $\frac{g_m}{g_e} = \frac{ \frac{GM_m}{R_m^2} }{ \frac{GM_e}{R_e^2} }$ $= \frac{M_m}{M_e} \times \left( \frac{R_e}{R_m} \right)^2$ By substituting the values, we get $\frac{g_m}{g_e} = \frac{1}{10} \times \left( \frac{6400}{3200} \right)^2 = \frac{1}{10} \times 4$ $\Rightarrow g_m = \frac{2}{5} g_e$ Given, the weight on earth's surface, $w_e = m g_e = 200 \text{N}$ ∴ Weight on the Mars surface, $w_m = m g_m = \frac{2}{5} (m g_e)$ $= \frac{2}{5} \times 200 \text{N} = 80 \text{N}$ © examsnet.com

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Given, gravitational field intensity, $\mathbf{I} = (5\hat{i}+12\hat{j})\,\mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$ Mass of object, $m=3\,\mathrm{kg}$ We know that, change in potential energy from to $P(8\,\mathrm{m},-2\,\mathrm{m})$ is given by $\Delta U = m \Delta V = m \int\limits_{(0,0)}^{(8,-2)} \mathbf{I} \cdot d\mathbf{r}$ $=3 \int\limits_{(0,0)}^{(8,-2)} (5\hat{i}+12\hat{j}) \cdot (dx\,\hat{i}+dy\,\hat{j})$ $=3\left[5x+12y\right]_{(0,0)}^{(8,-2)}$ $\Delta U = 3[40-24] = 48\,\mathrm{J}$ © examsnet.com

question: One thousand small water drops of equal radii combine to form a big drop. The ratio of final surface energy to total initial surface energy is ______

solution: Solution: Let radius of big drop $=R$ Radius of small drop $=T$ Number of small drops, $n=1000$ In this process, the volume remains same $V_{f}=V_{i}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{4}{3} \pi R^{3}=n\left(\frac{4}{3} \pi r^{3}\right)$ $\Rightarrow R^{3}=1000 r^{3} \Rightarrow R=10r$ ...(i) Initial surface area, $A_{1}=n 4 \pi r^{2}$ Final surface area, $A_{2}=4 \pi R^{2}$ Now, increase in surface area, $\Delta A=A_{2}-A_{1}=4 \pi [R^{2}-n r^{2}]$ We know that, surface energy, $SE = TA$ [where, $T=$ surface tension of liquid $]$ According to question. $\frac{SE_{f}}{SE_{i}}=\frac{TA_{2}}{TA_{1}}=\frac{4 \pi R^{2}}{n(4 \pi r^{2})}$ $=\frac{R^{2}}{1000 r^{2}}$ [From Eq. (i)] $=\frac{(10 r)^{2}}{1000 r^{2}}=\frac{100 r^{2}}{1000 r^{2}}=\frac{1}{10}$ or $1:10$ © examsnet.com

question: If the ratio of amplitudes of two interfering waves is $4:3$ , then the ratio of maximum and minimum intensity is:

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Given, the ratio of amplitudes of two interfering waves is $4:3$ i.e., $\frac{A_{1}}{A_{2}}=\frac{4}{3}$ We know that, intensity of wave is proportional to square of amplitude. $\therefore \frac{I_{max}}{I_{min}} = \left(\frac{A_{max}}{A_{min}}\right)^{2}$ , where maximum and minimum amplitudes are $A_{max} = A_{1}+A_{2}$ and $A_{min} = A_{1}-A_{2}$ Substituting the values, we get $\frac{I_{max}}{I_{min}} = \left(\frac{A_{1}+A_{2}}{A_{1}-A_{2}}\right)^{2}$ Multiplying and dividing by $A_{2}^{2}$ in RHS, we get. $\frac{I_{max}}{I_{min}} = \left( \frac{ \frac{A_{1}}{A_{2}} + 1 }{ \frac{A_{1}}{A_{2}} - 1 } \right)^{2}$ $= \left( \frac{ \frac{4}{3} + 1 }{ \frac{4}{3} - 1 } \right)^{2}$ $= \left( \frac{7}{1} \right)^{2} = \frac{49}{1}$ © examsnet.com

question: Assertion (A): Two condensers of same capacity are connected first in parallel and then in series.   The ratio of resultant capacities in the two cases will be $4:1$ Reason (R): In parallel, capacity increases and in series capacity decreases

options.A: Both $A$ and $R$ are true and $R$ is a correct explanation for $A$
options.B: Both $A$ and $R$ are true but $R$ is not a correct explanation for $A$

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Given, two capacitors of same capacities $C$ . In series, equivalent capacitance is given by $\frac{1}{C_S}=\frac{1}{C_1}+\frac{1}{C_2}=\frac{1}{C}+\frac{1}{C}=\frac{2}{C}$ $C_S = \frac{C}{2}$ In parallel, equivalent capacitance is given by $C_P = C_1 + C_2 = C + C = 2C$ Ratio $= \frac{C_P}{C_S} = \frac{2C}{\left(\frac{C}{2}\right)} = \frac{4}{1}$ $\Rightarrow C_P: C_S = 4:1$ Hence, Assertion is true. In parallel, $C_P > C$ In series, $C_S < C$ So, in parallel, capacity is increased but in series, capacity is decreased. Hence, Reason is also true, but it is not the correct explanation of  Assertion. © examsnet.com

question: Which of the following is false?

options.A: If $f$ is an even function from $R$ to $R$ then $f(o)$ must be equal to 0
options.B: $f: R \rightarrow R$ defined by $f(x)=x-[x] \forall x \in R$ , where $[x]$ is the greatest integer not greater than $x$ , is a periodic function
options.C: If $f: R \rightarrow R$ is an odd function, then $f(o)=0$
options.D: Number of onto functions from $\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$ to $\{1,2\}$ is 62

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: If f is an even function from R to R, then $f(0)$ must be equal to 0. ∵  We know that if a function $f(x)$ is even, then $f(-x)=f(x)$ Now, if we assume $f(x)=\cos x$ $f(-x)=\cos(-x)$ $=\cos x$ $\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;$ $\{\because \cos(-\theta)=(\cos \theta)\}$ $=f(x)$ ∴ $f(x)=\cos x$ is an even function. Now, $f(0)=\cos 0=1 \neq 0$ The given statement is false. (b) $f: R \rightarrow R, f(x)=x-[x]$ ∵ We know that, $x=[x]+\{x\}$ where $\{x\}=$ fractional part function $\Rightarrow x-[x]=\{x\}$ $\therefore f(x)=\{x\}$ where $\{x\}$ is a periodic function. $\Rightarrow f(x)$ is periodic function. ∴ The given statement is true. (c) $f: R \rightarrow R$ is an odd function, then $f(0)=0$ We know that if $f(x)$ is an odd function, then $f(-x)=-f(x)$ Put $x=0$ , we get $f(0)=-f(0)$ $\Rightarrow f(0)+f(0)=0$ $2 f(0)=0$ $\Rightarrow f(0)=0$ The given statement is true. (d) Number of onto functions from $\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$ to $\{1,2\}$ is 62. Let $A=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$ and $B=\{1,2\}$ ∵ $\Rightarrow n(A)=6$ and $n(B)=2$ ∵  We know that the number of onto function from a set A with m number of elements to set B with n number of elements is $n^{m}-\{{}^{n}C_{1}(n-1)^{m}+{}^{n}C_{2}(n-2)^{m}+\dots{}^{n}C_{n-1}(1)^{m}\}$ Here n = 2 and m = 6 So, total number of onto function are $2^{6}-\{{}^{2}C_{1}(2-1)^{6}+{}^{2}C_{2}(2-2)^{6}]$ $=64-[2+0]$ $=64-2=62$ ∴ The given statement is true. © examsnet.com

question: Let $z=\cos \theta+i \sin \theta$ . Then the value of $\sum\limits_{m=1}^{15} I_{m}(z^{2m-1})$ at $\theta=2^{\circ}$ is

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: $z=\cos \theta+i \sin \theta=e^{i \theta}\;\;\;\;\;$ [in Euler's form] Using Demoivre theorem $z^{2}=\cos 2\theta+i \sin 2\theta$ $z^{3}=\cos 3\theta+i \sin 3\theta$ Now, according to the question $\sum\limits_{m=1}^{15} I_{m}(z^{2m-1})$ ⇒ Imaginary part of $(z+z^{3}+z^{5}+...+z^{29})$ ⇒ $\sin \theta+\sin 3\theta+\sin 5\theta+...\sin 29\theta)$ $\Rightarrow \frac{\sin 15 \frac{2\theta}{2}}{\sin \frac{2\theta}{2}}\left[\sin \left(\theta+(15-1)\frac{2\theta}{2}\right)\right]$ $[\because \sin \alpha+\sin (\alpha+\beta)+\dots$ to $n \text{term}$ $=\frac{\sin \frac{n\beta}{2}}{\sin \frac{\beta}{2}}\left[\sin \left(\alpha+(n-1)\frac{\beta}{2}\right)\right]$ Here, $\alpha=\theta, \beta=2\theta, n=15]$ $\Rightarrow \frac{\sin 15\theta}{\sin \theta} \cdot \sin (15\theta)$ Now, $\theta=2^{\circ}$ $=\frac{\sin 30^{\circ} \sin 30^{\circ}}{\sin 2^{\circ}}=\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{\sin 2^{\circ}}$ $=\frac{1}{4\sin 2^{\circ}}$ © examsnet.com

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Equation $x^{2}-a x+b$ and $x^{2}+b x-a$ have $a$ common root. Let $\alpha$ be the common root of both quadratic equations $\Rightarrow \alpha^{2}-a \alpha+b=0$ $\alpha^{2}+b \alpha-a=0$ Using cross-multiplication $\frac{\alpha^{2}}{\begin{array}{cc} -a & b \\ b & -a \end{array}} = \frac{\alpha}{\begin{array}{cc} b & 1 \\ -a & 1 \end{array}} = \frac{1}{\begin{array}{cc} 1 & -a \\ 1 & b \end{array}}$ $\frac{\alpha^{2}}{a^{2}-b^{2}} = \frac{\alpha}{b+a} = \frac{1}{b+a}$ We get $\frac{\alpha}{b+a} = \frac{1}{b+a}$ $\Rightarrow \alpha=1$ Now, using first two fraction $\frac{1}{a^{2}-b^{2}} = \frac{1}{a+b}$ $\Rightarrow a+b=a^{2}-b^{2}$ $\Rightarrow (a+b)=(a+b)(a-b)$ $\Rightarrow (a+b)(a-b-1)=0$ $a+b=0$ or $a-b-1=0$ $\Rightarrow a-b=1$ © examsnet.com

solution: Solution: $C_{1}: x^{2}+y^{2}+x+y-4=0$ $C_{2}: 3 x^{2}+3 y^{2}-x-y-\lambda=0$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}+y^{2}-\frac{x}{3}-\frac{y}{3}-\frac{\lambda}{3}=0$ ∴ Length of tangent drawn by an external point is $\sqrt{S_1}$ . ∴ Length of tangent drawn from $(1,2)$ to $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ are $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ respectively. $L_{1}=\sqrt{S_{1}}=\sqrt{1^{2}+2^{2}+1+2-4}$ $=\sqrt{1+4+1+2-4}=\sqrt{4}$ $L_{1}=2$ $\therefore L_{2}=\sqrt{S_{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{1^{2}+2^{2}-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{2}{3}-\frac{\lambda}{3}}$ $=\sqrt{4-\frac{\lambda}{3}}$ Given that, $\frac{L_{1}}{L_{2}}=\frac{3}{4}$ $=\frac{2}{\sqrt{4-\frac{\lambda}{3}}}=\frac{3}{4}$ $\Rightarrow 3 \sqrt{4-\frac{\lambda}{3}}=8$ $\Rightarrow 9\left(4-\frac{\lambda}{3}\right)=64$ $\Rightarrow 4-\frac{\lambda}{3}=\frac{64}{9}$ $\Rightarrow 4-\frac{64}{9}=\frac{\lambda}{3}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{36-64}{9}=\frac{\lambda}{3}$ $\lambda=-\frac{28}{3}$ © examsnet.com

(i) and (ii), we get $2 I = \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \frac{x \tan x+(\pi-x) \tan x}{\sec x+\tan x} d x$ $2 I = \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\pi \tan x}{\sec x+\tan x} d x$ $I = \frac{\pi}{2} \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\tan x}{\sec x+\tan x} d x = \frac{\pi}{2} \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}}{\frac{1}{\cos x}+\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}} d x$ $= \frac{\pi}{2} \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \left( \frac{\sin x}{1+\sin x} \times \frac{1-\sin x}{1-\sin x} \right) d x$ $= \frac{\pi}{2} \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\sin x(1-\sin x)}{1-\sin^{2} x} d x$ $= \frac{\pi}{2} \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\sin x - \sin^{2} x}{\cos^{2} x} d x$ $I = \frac{\pi}{2} \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \left( \frac{\sin x}{\cos^{2} x} - \frac{\sin^{2} x}{\cos^{2} x} \right) d x$ $\frac{\pi}{2} \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \left( \sec x \tan x - \tan^{2} x \right) d x$ $\frac{\pi}{2} \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \left\{ \sec x \tan x - (\sec^{2} x - 1) \right\} d x$ $I = \frac{\pi}{2} \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \left( \sec x \tan x - \sec^{2} x + 1 \right) d x$ $= \frac{\pi}{2} \left[ \sec x - \tan x + x \right]_{0}^{\pi}$ $= \frac{\pi}{2} \left\{ (\sec \pi - \tan \pi + \pi) - \frac{\pi}{2} \right\}$ $\left\{ \sec 0^{\circ} - \tan 0^{\circ} + 0 \right\}$ $= \frac{\pi}{2} \left\{ (-1-0+\pi) - (1-0+0) \right\}$ $= \frac{\pi}{2} (\pi-1-1) = \frac{\pi}{2} (\pi-2)$ $I = \frac{\pi (\pi-2)}{2}$ © examsnet.com

solution: Solution: Given that, mass of rod $=m$ Length of rod, $L=21$ Initial and final angular velocities are 0 and $\omega$ respectively, Time taken $=t$ We know that, torque acting on body having moment of inertia $(I)$ and angular acceleration $(\alpha)$ is $\tau = l \alpha$ where, $I = \frac{1}{12} ML^{2} = \frac{1}{12} m(2)^{2}$ $= \frac{1}{3} m l^{2}$ and $\alpha = \frac{\omega_{f} - \omega_{i}}{t} = \frac{\omega - 0}{t} = \frac{\omega}{t}$ Now, substituting the values, we get $\tau = \frac{1}{3} m l^{2} \frac{\omega}{t}$ © examsnet.com

question: A flywheel having moment of inertia $10 \text{ kg} \cdot \text{m}^{2}$ is rotating at $50 \text{ rad} \cdot \text{s}^{-1}$ . What amount of work needs to be done in order to bring this flywheel to rest in 10 seconds?

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Given that, moment of inertia, $I=10 \text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^{2}$ Initial angular velocity, $\omega_{0}=50 \text{ rad} / \text{s}$ Final angular velocity, $\omega=0$ Time taken to stop wheel, $t=10 \text{ s}$ We know that, work done by torque = change of rotational KE $W=\Delta \text{KE}=K_f - K_i$ $W=\frac{1}{2} I \omega^{2} - \frac{1}{2} I \omega_{a}^{2}$ $W=0-\frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times (50)^{2}$ = -12500 J So, amount of work done to bring the flywheel to rest is $12500 \text{ J}$ . © examsnet.com

question: Two particles ' $P$ ' and ' $Q$ ' describe SHM of same amplitude ' $a$ ' and same frequency ' $f$ ' along the same straight line. The maximum distance between the two particles is $a \sqrt{2}$ . The phase difference between the particle is _____

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Given that, two particles P and Q describes SHM of same amplitude $a$ and frequency $f$ . Let equation of motion of two particles are $x_{1}=a \sin \omega t$ and $x_{2}=a \sin (\omega t + \phi)$ where, $\phi$ be the phase difference. ∴ Path difference, $x_{2}-x_{1}=a \sin (\omega t + \phi) - a \sin \omega t$ $x_{2}-x_{1}=2 a \sin \left( \frac{\omega t + \phi - \omega t}{2} \right) \cos \left( \frac{\omega t + \phi + \omega t}{2} \right)$ [Using identity $\sin A - \sin B = 2 \sin \left( \frac{A-B}{2} \right) \cdot \cos \left( \frac{A+B}{2} \right) ]$ ∴ $x_{2}-x_{1}=2 a \sin \left( \frac{\phi}{2} \right) \cos \left( \omega + \frac{\phi}{2} \right)$ The distance $x_{2}-x_{1}$ will be maximum when $\cos \left( \omega t + \frac{\phi}{2} \right) = 1$ ∴ Maximum distance $x_{2}-x_{1} = \sqrt{2} a$ $= 2 a \sin \frac{\phi}{2}$ $\Rightarrow \sin \frac{\phi}{2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ $\Rightarrow \sin \frac{\phi}{2} = \sin 45^{\circ}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{\phi}{2} = 45^{\circ}$ Phase difference, $\phi = 90^{\circ} = \frac{\pi}{2}$ © examsnet.com

solution: Solution: Given that, equation of a particle executing Simple harmonic motion is $x=A \cos \left(\omega t+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ Now, velocity of particle, $v=\frac{dx}{dt}$ $v=\frac{d}{dt}\left[A \cos \left(\omega t+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right]$ $=-A\omega \sin \left(\omega t+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ $v$ is maximum when $\sin \left(\omega t+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=1$ $\sin \left(\omega t+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\sin \frac{\pi}{2}$ $\Rightarrow \omega t+\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi}{2}$ $\Rightarrow t=\frac{\pi}{4\omega}$ © examsnet.com

question: A communication satellite of $500\ \mathrm{kg}$ revolves around the earth in a circular orbit of radius $4.0 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m}$ in the equatorial plane of the earth from west to east. The magnitude of angular momentum of the satellite is _____

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Given that, mass of satellite, $m=500\ \mathrm{kg}$ Radius of orbit, $r=4 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m}$ Now, the satellite is revolving in equatorial plane so, its time period will be equal to time period of  rotation of earth i.e., $T=24\ \mathrm{h}$ . ∴ Angular velocity of satellite, $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$ Now, angular momentum, $L = m \omega r^{2} = m \left(\frac{2\pi}{T}\right) r^{2}$ $= 500 \times \left(\frac{2\pi}{24 \times 3600}\right) \times (4 \times 10^{7})^{2}$ $= 0.58 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{kg} \cdot \mathrm{m}^{2} \cdot \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ © examsnet.com

solution: Solution: Given that, angle of laticude, $\lambda = 45^{\circ}$ We know that, the expression of gravity at latitude angle is $g_{\lambda} = g - \omega^{2} R \cos^{2} \lambda$ The weight of man of mass $m$ at this point $w = m g_{\lambda} = m(g - \omega^{2} R \cos^{2} 45^{\circ})$ According to question, man feels weightlessness ∴ w = 0 $m(g - \omega^{2} R \cos^{2} 45^{\circ}) = 0$ But $m \neq 0$ , then $g - \omega^{2} R \cos^{2} 45^{\circ} = 0$ $\Rightarrow \omega = \sqrt{\frac{2q}{R}}$ Now, using time period, (duration of day) $= T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{R}{2g}} = \pi \sqrt{\frac{2R}{g}}$ © examsnet.com

question: A body cools down from $52.5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $47.5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ in 5 minutes and from $47.5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $42.5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ in $7.5$ minute. Then the temperature of the surroundings is _______

solution: Solution: Given that, for first condition, Initial temperature, $T_{1}=52.5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ Final temperature, $T_{v}=47.5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ Average temperature, $T_{\mathrm{av}}=\frac{T_{1}+T_{2}}{2}$ $=\frac{525+47.5}{2}=50^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ For second condition, Initial temperature, $T_{1}=47.5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ Final temperature, $T_{2}=42.5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ Average temperature, $T_{\mathrm{av}}=\frac{T_{1}+T_{2}}{2}$ $=\frac{47.5+42.5}{2}=45^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ Let $T_{0}$ be the temperature of surroundings. Now, using expression of rate of cooling, $R=\frac{\Delta T}{\Delta}=-K(T_{\mathrm{av}}-T_{0})$ Substituting the values in above equation from $1^{\text{st}}$ and 2nd conditions, we get $\frac{T_{1}-T_{2}}{t_{1}}=-K(T_{\mathrm{av}}-T_{0})$ $\frac{52.5-47.5}{5}=-K(50-T_{0})$ ...(i) Similarly, $\frac{47,5-42.5}{7.5}=-K(45-T_{0})$ ...(ii) Dividing Eq. (i) by Eq. (ii), we get $\frac{\frac{52.5-47.5}{5}}{\frac{47.5-42.5}{7.5}}=\frac{-K(50-T_{0})}{-K(45-T_{0})}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{5}{5} \times \frac{7.5}{5} = \frac{50-T_{0}}{45-T_{0}}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{3}{2} = \frac{50-T_{0}}{45-T_{0}}$ $T_{0}=35^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ Hence, the temperature of surroundings is $35^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . © examsnet.com

All middle terms cancel, so $=\frac{1}{\sin1^\circ}(\cot45^\circ-\cot90^\circ)$ . Since $\cot45^\circ=1$ and $\cot90^\circ=0$ , $=\frac{1}{\sin1^\circ}=\csc1^\circ$ . solution: Solution: In a regular hexagon $ABCDEF$ , let $\overrightarrow{AB}=\vec{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}=\vec{b}$ . Using vector addition, $\overrightarrow{AC}=\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BC}=\vec{a}+\vec{b}$ . In a regular hexagon, $\overrightarrow{AD}$ is parallel to $\overrightarrow{BC}$ and has twice its length, so $\overrightarrow{AD}=2\vec{b}$ . Therefore $\overrightarrow{CD}=\overrightarrow{AD}-\overrightarrow{AC}=2\vec{b}-(\vec{a}+\vec{b})=\vec{b}-\vec{a}$ . Also, $\overrightarrow{DE}$ is opposite to $\overrightarrow{AB}$ , so $\overrightarrow{DE}=-\vec{a}$ . Thus $\overrightarrow{CE}=\overrightarrow{CD}+\overrightarrow{DE}=(\vec{b}-\vec{a})+(-\vec{a})=\vec{b}-2\vec{a}$ . solution: Solution: We have, $I=\int\limits_{0}^{\pi} x\{\sin^{2}(\sin x)+\cos^{2}(\cos x)\}\,dx$ $I=\int\limits_{0}^{\pi}(\pi-x)[\sin^{2}(\sin(\pi-x)]+\cos^{2}(\cos(\pi-x))\,dx$ $I=\int\limits_{0}^{\pi}(\pi-x)[\sin^{2}(\sin x)+\cos^{2}(\cos x)]\,dx$ $2I=\pi\int\limits_{0}^{\pi}[\sin^{2}(\sin x)+\cos^{2}(\cos x)]\,dx$ $I=\pi\int\limits_{0}^{\pi}[\sin^{2}(\sin x)+\cos^{2}(\cos x)]\,dx$ $\left[\because\int\limits_{0}^{2} f(x)\,dx=2\int\limits_{0}^{a} f(x)\,dx\right]$ $I=\pi\int\limits_{0}^{\pi/2}\left[\sin^{2}\left(\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)\right)+\cos^{2}\left(\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)\right)\right]\,dx$ $I=\pi\int\limits_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin^{2}(\cos x)+\cos^{2}(\sin x)\,dx$ $2l=\pi\int\limits_{0}^{\pi/2} 2\,dx$ $\Rightarrow I=\pi\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=\frac{\pi^{2}}{2}$ $[I]=\left[\frac{\pi^{2}}{2}\right]=4\;\;\;\;$ $\left[\begin{array}{ll}\because \pi^2 & \in (9,10) \\ \frac{\pi^2}{2} & \in (4.5,5) \end{array}\right]$ © examsnet.com

solution: Solution: Given that, mass of oxygen, $m_{0}=16\ \mathrm{amu}$ Mass of carbon, $m_{c}=12\ \mathrm{amu}$ Distance between them, $r=11\,\text{\AA}$ Let $x$ be the distance of centre of mass from carbon atom By using expression of centre of mass for two particle system, $X_{com}=\frac{m_{1} x_{t}+m_{2} x_{2}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}$ Assuming centre of mass at orgin, we get $X_{COM}=0=\frac{m_{C}(-x)+m_{O}(r-x)}{m_{c}+m_{O}}$ $m_{c} x=m_{o}(r-x)$ $m_{c} x+m_{0} x=m_{0} r$ $x=\frac{m_{o}}{m_{c}+m_{o}} r$ By substituting the values, we get $x=\frac{16}{16+12} \times (1.1) \text{\AA} =0.63 \text{\AA}$ Hence, position of centre of mass is $0.63 \text{\AA}$ from carbon atom. © examsnet.com

question: Match the following? Column-I Column-II (a) Ratio of $\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta U}$ in an isobaric process (i) $\frac{T_{1}}{T_{1}-T_{2}}$ (b) Ratio of $\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta W}$ in an isobaric process (ii) $\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}-T_{2}}$ (c) Coefficient of performance of a refrigerator (iii) $\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}$ ;(d) Coefficient of performance of a heat pump (iv) $\gamma$

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: We know that, at constant volume, Heat supplicd, $\Delta Q_{1}=\Delta U=C_{y} \Delta T$ At constant pressure, heat supplied, $\Delta Q=C \cdot \Delta T=\Delta U+\Delta W$ Ratio of heat capacity at constant pressure to constant volume is $\gamma=\frac{C_{r}}{C_{y}}$ Now, $\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta U}=\frac{C_{p} \Delta T}{C_{V} \Delta T}=\frac{C_{p}}{C_{V}}=\gamma$ $\text{Now}, \frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta W}=\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta Q-\Delta U}$ $=\frac{C_{p} \Delta T}{C_{p} \Delta T-C_{V} \Delta T}$ $=\frac{C_{r}}{C_{p}-C_{v}}=\frac{C_{p}}{C_{v}\left(\frac{C_{p}}{C_{v}}-1\right)}$ $=\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}$ For refrigerator, coefficient of performance, $\beta=\frac{Q_{2}}{W}=\frac{\text{Heat absorbed from food stuff}}{\text{Electrical work done}}$ ∴ $\beta=\frac{Q_{2}}{Q_{1}-Q_{2}}$ Coefficient of heat pump $=\frac{\text{Heat released}}{\text{Electrical work}}$ i.e. $\alpha=\frac{Q_{1}}{W}=\frac{Q_{4}}{Q_{1}-Q_{2}}$ We know that, $\frac{Q_{1}}{Q_{2}}=\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}$ So, we get, $\beta=\frac{Q_{2}}{Q_{1}-Q_{2}}=\frac{\frac{Q_{2}}{Q_{4}}}{1-\frac{Q_{2}}{Q_{1}}}$ $=\frac{\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}}{1-\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}}=\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}-T_{2}}$ and $\alpha=\frac{Q}{Q_{1}-Q_{2}}$ $=\frac{\frac{Q_{1}}{Q_{2}}}{\frac{Q_{1}}{Q_{2}}-1}=\frac{\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}}{\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}-1}$ $=\frac{T_{1}}{T_{1}-T_{2}}$ Hence, we get the best match as given by $A \rightarrow 4, B \rightarrow 3, C \rightarrow 2$ and $D \rightarrow 1$ . © examsnet.com

question: A magnetic field given by $B(t)=(0.2\,t-0.05\,t^{2})\,\mathrm{T}$ is directed perpendicular to the plane of a circular coil containing 25 turns of radius $1.8\,\mathrm{cm}$ and whose total resistance is $5\ \Omega$ . The power dissipation at 3 seconds is nearly ______

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Given that, number of turns, $N=25$ Radius of coil, $r=1.8\,\mathrm{cm}=1.8\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}$ Resistance of coil, $R=5\ \Omega$ Magnetic field, $B=(0.2\,t-0.05\,t^{2})\,\mathrm{T}$ Now, area of coil, $A=\pi r^{2}=3.14\times(1.8\times10^{-2})^{2}$ $=1.02\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}^{2}$ Induced emf, $\varepsilon = \frac{-Nd}{d t}(BA) = -NA \frac{dB}{d t}$ $= -NA \frac{d}{d t}(0.2t-0.05t^{2})$ $\varepsilon = -NA(0.2-0.1t)$ Substituting the values, we get $\varepsilon = -25 \times 1.02 \times 10^{-3} (0.2-0.1t)$ $= -2.55 \times 10^{-2} (0.2-0.1t)$ Now, instantaneous power, $P = \frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{R} = \frac{[-2.55 \times 10^{-2} (0.2-0.1t)]^{2}}{5}$ At, $t=35$ , power dissipated is $P = \frac{(2.55 \times 10^{-2})^{2}(0.2-0.1 \times 3)^{2}}{5}$ $= 1.30 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{W} = 1.30 \mu \mathrm{W}$ It is close to option $(d)$ . © examsnet.com

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: We have, ${}^{7}P_{3}-3^{6}P_{2}$ $\frac{7!}{4!}-3\cdot\frac{6!}{4!}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{7!}{4!}-\frac{3\cdot6!}{4!}$ $= \frac{6!}{4!}(7-3) = \frac{6!}{4!} \times 4$ $= \frac{6! \times 4}{4 \times 3!} = \frac{6!}{3!} = {}^{6}P_{3}$ © examsnet.com

question: If $\frac{x}{(1+x^{2})(3-2x)}=\frac{Bx+C}{1+x^{2}}+\frac{A}{3-2x}$ , then ' $C$ ' is

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: We have, $\frac{x}{(1+x^{2})(3-2x)}=\frac{Bx+C}{1+x^{2}}+\frac{A}{(3-2x)}$ $\Rightarrow\frac{x}{(1+x^{2})(3-2x)}=\frac{Bx(3-2x)+C(3-2x)+A(1+x^{2})}{(1+x^{2})(3-2x)}$ $\Rightarrow x=Bx(3-2x)+C(3-2x)+A(1+x^{2})$ $\Rightarrow x=3Bx-2Bx^{2}+3C-2Cx+A+Ax^{2}$ $\Rightarrow x=(A-2B)x^{2}+(3B-2C)x+A+3C$ Equating the coefficient of $x^{2}, x$ and constant term $A-2B=0,3B-2C=1,A+3C=0$ Solving, we get $A=\frac{6}{13}, B=\frac{3}{13}, C=-\frac{2}{13}$ ∴ $C=-\frac{2}{13}$ © examsnet.com
